output.brief: The gap is mostly a tenure effect, not a location effect. Remote hiring only opened to all roles in July 2024, so most remote staff are new: 230 of 340 haven't reached the 18 months in level that the policy requires to be nominated, against 200 of 760 office staff. Among eligible staff, nomination rates (28.6% vs 28.2%) and approval rates (73.8% vs 71.0%) are almost the same. Applying office rates to the remote tenure mix predicts 8.2%, close to the observed 7.6%. Remote staff don't leave more often (10.9% vs 11.6%), and the gap shows up in every job family, so job mix isn't the cause. I'm fairly confident, though the eligible remote group is only 110 people, so a modest real bias can't be ruled out. Stretch-assignment access is unmeasured; the manager comments hint at it but don't establish it. Don't adopt the three-day office rule: it would penalise about 180 remote staff hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misread comparison. Instead, put it on hold, report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at FY2027. Consider pulling staffing records to test the stretch-work question.
